items.prompt: The module opens by tracing one `set(updater)` call through eight hand-offs. Which sequence matches the order the trace gives for the store side (steps 2 to 5)?

options.text: The updater runs against the current `state`; `Object.is` compares its return value with `state`; `previousState` is captured and the replace-or-merge assignment runs; then every listener is called.
The updater runs against the current `state`; the replace-or-merge assignment runs; `Object.is` compares the merged result with `previousState`; every listener is called only if the two differ.
The updater runs against the current `state`; `Object.is` compares its return value with `state`; every listener is called with `(nextState, state)`; then the replace-or-merge assignment runs.

The updater runs against the current `state`; the replace-or-merge assignment runs; there is no store-level bail-out, so every listener is called and React's per-component comparison alone filters renders.

items.whyHard: The compare-after-merge sequence is the design most engineers assume (compare the final state with the previous one) and it is wrong in a way that matters: `Object.assign({}, ...)` always yields a fresh object, so a compare-after-merge could never bail out. The trace's step 3 compares the updater's RETURN VALUE with the current state before any merge, which is exactly why returning `state` itself bails and returning `{ ...state }` notifies everyone. Notify-before-assign and no-bail-out-at-all are also coherent designs; only the module fixes the order.

items.prompt: Steps 6 and 7 describe what `useStore` hands to `React.useSyncExternalStore`. Which description matches the module?

options.text: `api.subscribe` unchanged, plus two memoized readers, `() => selector(api.getState())` and `() => selector(api.getInitialState())`; the selector runs inside the snapshot readers.
`api.subscribe`, `api.getState` and `api.getInitialState` unchanged; the hook returns the whole state object and `useStore` applies `selector` to that returned value afterward.
A wrapped subscribe that invokes React's callback only when `selector(api.getState())` has changed, plus `api.getState` as the single snapshot reader; the selector runs in the wrapper.
`api.subscribe`, a memoized `() => selector(api.getState())`, and `Object.is` passed as an `isEqual` argument; that third argument is how React decides whether the selected slice changed.

items.whyHard: Every option is a workable binding. The `isEqual` option lifts a real parameter from `useSyncExternalStoreWithSelector`, the shim zustand actually used from #550 until #2301, so an engineer who remembers that era will reach for it. Selecting after the read, or filtering inside subscribe, are both how people build this by hand. Only the module states that BOTH snapshot readers wrap the selector and that the second one reads `getInitialState`, the server-snapshot slot.

items.prompt: Step 4 of the trace is the replace-or-merge decision. For `set(nextState, replace)`, how does the module say that decision is made?

options.text: An explicit `replace` wins (`true` assigns wholesale, `false` merges); only when it is omitted does the fallback apply: a non-object or `null` is assigned, an object is merged one level deep.
The type check wins outright: a non-object or `null` is always assigned wholesale; `replace` is consulted only for object values, where `true` assigns and `false` or omitted merges one level deep.
An explicit `replace: true` assigns wholesale; otherwise the object is merged recursively, so a nested object you did not spread keeps its untouched keys instead of being replaced.
`replace` defaults to `true` when the updater form `set(fn)` is used, since the function is expected to return the full state; the plain-object form defaults to a one-level merge.

items.whyHard: The two precedence variants differ only in `replace ?? typeCheck` versus `typeCheck || replace`, and the observable difference (`set(5, false)` merges into a copy of state under the real formula, becomes `5` under the swapped one) is invisible unless you read the formula quoted in step 4. Deep merge is the assumption people carry from immer-style libraries, and a replace-by-default updater form is a convention other stores really use.

items.prompt: The module's warning box is precise about how zustand handles the 'zombie child' pitfall today versus in the past. Which account matches it?

options.text: Until April 2022 it was hand-rolled with `useReducer` plus refs that re-checked state after subscribing; #550 deleted that in favor of the `use-sync-external-store` shim, and #2301 (Jan 2024) moved to `React.useSyncExternalStore` directly.

Until April 2022 it was hand-rolled with `useReducer` plus refs that re-checked state after subscribing; #550 deleted that and called `React.useSyncExternalStore` directly, and #2301 (Jan 2024) swapped in the `use-sync-external-store` shim for React 17.

It has always been structural: `src/react.ts` never uses React context, so a subscribed child cannot read a stale value from a provider; #550 and #2301 only changed where `useSyncExternalStore` is imported from, nothing else.

Until April 2022 it relied on React's experimental `useMutableSource`; #550 replaced that with the `use-sync-external-store` shim once React 18 shipped, and #2301 (Jan 2024) moved to `React.useSyncExternalStore` directly.

items.whyHard: All four use real identifiers. The swapped-PR account keeps the correct mechanism but reverses which PR introduced the shim and which removed it (the module gives both PR numbers and dates, and React 18 shipping two weeks before #550 makes a direct call in 2022 sound right). The context-free account is the module's explanation of a DIFFERENT pitfall, context loss, which the warning box deliberately separates from zombie children. The `useMutableSource` account borrows the RFC that the introduction doc links for concurrency.

items.prompt: `useBear` is both a hook and a handle: `useBear.getState()` works outside React. Which statement matches the module on what `create` staples onto the hook, and how?

options.text: `setState`, `getState`, `getInitialState` and `subscribe`, copied as own properties by `Object.assign(useBoundStore, api)` once the vanilla store has been built.
`setState`, `getState`, `subscribe` and `destroy`, copied as own properties by `Object.assign(useBoundStore, api)` once the vanilla store has been built.
`getState`, `getInitialState` and `subscribe` only, the `ReadonlyStoreApi` subset; `setState` stays off the hook so that writes have to go through the store's actions.
`setState`, `getState`, `getInitialState` and `subscribe`, inherited through the prototype because the hook is built with `Object.create(api)` rather than having them copied on.

items.whyHard: The `destroy` option is the v4 surface (removed in v5 by #2235) and reads identically otherwise, so anyone whose zustand knowledge predates v5 picks it. The read-only subset mirrors the `ReadonlyStoreApi` type that appears in `useStore`'s own signature earlier in the module, so a skimmer who saw that type would pick it. Prototype inheritance is a plausible mechanism for the same four names. Only the module's snippet and its explicit list settle both WHICH four and HOW.
